evidence.claim: The approach from the east developed from a rough coastal trail into a wagon road in the 1920s.
evidence.quote: a rough trail along the Strait of Juan de Fuca was used by American emigrants. The trail was upgraded to a wagon road in the 1920s

evidence.quote: SR 112 begins at the eastern boundary of the Makah Indian Reservation near the mouth of the Sail River. The highway continues west as Bayview Avenue

evidence.quote: The museum includes a replica long house and thousands of artifacts of interest to academics and laypeople, including canoes, basketry, whaling and fishing gear.

evidence.claim: The forest trail reaches the place where the Strait of Juan de Fuca meets the Pacific Ocean, the northwesternmost point of the contiguous United States.
evidence.quote: Cape Flattery (48°23′09″N 124°43′37″W) is the northwesternmost point of the contiguous United States. It is in Clallam County, Washington, on the Olympic Peninsula, where the Strait of Juan de Fuca joins the Pacific Ocean.

flags: Tourism pages call this the first tribal road with national scenic status; the highway article calls it a state byway and identifies the separate Strait of Juan de Fuca Highway as nationally designated. Formal tier and first-in-nation claim omitted pending designation record.

Tourism sources describe the corridor loosely as SR 112, but highway source ends numbered SR 112 at the reservation boundary and continues west as Bayview Avenue. History explicitly concerns the eastern approach, not construction of the tribal road.
Tourism distance is 12 miles; material maps 34.4 miles and reverses the strip order. Used the tourism corridor east-to-west, with museum before cape and offshore view.

Ozette mudslide dates conflict across caches (around 1750 versus roughly 1560 or 1700). Date omitted. No direct Makah-authored page is cached; cultural history is limited to museum objects and documented tribal leadership.
Corrected tourism page’s northernmost to northwesternmost using the other sources. Removed the redundant only-road superlative, although tourism supports it.

Tatoosh retains title, coordinates and lighthouse motif; short walk refers to the mainland viewpoint, not island access. The original coordinates mark the lighthouse, not the island centroid, and were preserved as required.
Practical checked date records review of saved tourism text only, not live verification or permission to visit. Museum moment is concise because its dedicated cache is brief.
